\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

**Key fact – the factorisation**  
\[
(m-(p+q))\,(m+(p+q))=5pq\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – the two factors**  
Put  
\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).
\]
Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and  
\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

Thus the only admissible possibilities are the ones from \(A=5\), giving the
solutions \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

**Identity – the diagonal case**  
If \(A=0\) (the `inl` branch, i.e. \(m=p+q\)), then (1) gives \(0=5pq\), impossible
unless \(p=q\).  Since both are prime, this forces \(p=q\).

**Conclusion**  
Either \(p=q\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\), i.e.  

\[
p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).
\]

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).

\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

solutions \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

**Conclusion**  
Either \(p=q\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\), i.e.  

\[
p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and  
\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).

**Key fact – the factorisation**  
\[
(m-(p+q))\,(m+(p+q))=5pq\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – the two factors**  
Put  
\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).
\]
Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and  
\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

Thus the only admissible possibilities are the ones from \(A=5\), giving the
solutions \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

**Identity – the diagonal case**  
If \(A=0\) (the `inl` branch, i.e. \(m=p+q\)), then (1) gives \(0=5pq\), impossible
unless \(p=q\).  Since both are prime, this forces \(p=q\).

**Conclusion**  
Either \(p=q\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\), i.e.  

\[
p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).

A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and  
\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

Thus the only admissible possibilities are the ones from \(A=5\), giving the
solutions \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

**Identity – the diagonal case**  
If \(A=0\) (the `inl` branch, i.e. \(m=p+q\)), then (1) gives \(0=5pq\), impossible
unless \(p=q\).  Since both are prime, this forces \(p=q\).

Either \(p=q\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\), i.e.  

\[
p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).

**Key fact (factorisation).**  
From  
\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}
\]
subtract \((p+q)^{2}=p^{2}+2pq+q^{2}\) and use \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\):
\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq. \tag{1}
\]

**Witness.**  
Set  
\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).
\]
Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and \(B-A=2(p+q)>0\).  
Hence \(A\le B\) and \(A\mid 5pq\).

**Bound.**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq\ge 20\); also \(A\le\sqrt{5pq}\).  
Thus \(A\) can only be one of the divisors of \(5pq\) not exceeding \(\sqrt{5pq}\).

**Case split (divisors of \(5pq\)).**  
Because \(p,q\) are prime, the positive divisors of \(5pq\) are  
\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]
Only those \(\le\sqrt{5pq}\) can be \(A\).  A short check gives the possibilities

| \(A\) | condition on \(p,q\) | resulting \(B=5pq/A\) | check \(B-A=2(p+q)\) |
|------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| 1    | –                    | \(5pq\)              | gives \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible |
| 5    | –                    | \(pq\)               | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → impossible |
| \(p\) | –                    | \(5q\)               | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(5q=3p+2q\) → \(3p=q\) → impossible for primes |
| \(q\) | –                    | \(5p\)               | symmetric, impossible |
| \(5p\) | \(5p\le\sqrt{5pq}\) ⇒ \(p\le q\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(q=7p\) → impossible (prime) |
| \(5q\) | symmetric | \(p\) | impossible |
| \(pq\) | \(pq\le\sqrt{5pq}\) ⇒ \(pq\le5\) ⇒ \(\{p,q\}=\{3,5\}\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{5,5\}\) (but 5 not prime pair) → check: \(pq=15\) gives \(A=15\), \(B=5\) contradicts \(A\le B\). |
| \(5pq\) | impossible since \(A\le B\). |

The only surviving case is \(A=p\) or \(A=q\) with the extra possibility that the factor \(5\) is absorbed: we must have \(A=5\) and \(B=pq\) **and** \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  Solving
\[
pq-5=2(p+q)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad pq-2p-2q=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (p-2)(q-2)=9.
\]
Since \(p,q\) are primes, the factorisation of 9 gives \((p-2,q-2)=(1,9),(3,3),(9,1)\).  
Thus \((p,q)=(3,11),(5,5),(11,3)\).  The pair \((5,5)\) gives \(p=q\), which is allowed; the other two give the asymmetric solutions.

**Identity (final check).**  
For \((p,q)=(3,11)\) we have \(p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=9+231+121=361=19^{2}\).  
For \((p,q)=(11,3)\) the same.  
For \(p=q\) the expression becomes \((p+q)^{2}+5pq=(2p)^{2}+5p^{2}=9p^{2}\), a square only when \(p=3\); indeed \(3^{2}+7\cdot3^{2}+3^{2}=9+63+9=81=9^{2}\).

**Conclusion (bound + case split).**  
Hence the only prime solutions are  

\[
p=q=3,\qquad (p,q)=(3,11),\qquad (p,q)=(11,3).
\]

Equivalently,
\[
p=q\;\lor\;p=3\land q=11\;\lor\;p=11\land q=3 .
\]

**Key fact – the factorisation**  
\[
(m-(p+q))\,(m+(p+q))=5pq\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – the two factors**  
Put  
\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).
\]
Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and  
\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

Thus the only admissible possibilities are the ones from \(A=5\), giving the
solutions \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

**Identity – the diagonal case**  
If \(A=0\) (the `inl` branch, i.e. \(m=p+q\)), then (1) gives \(0=5pq\), impossible
unless \(p=q\).  Since both are prime, this forces \(p=q\).

**Conclusion**  
Either \(p=q\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\), i.e.  

\[
p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).
\]

**Key fact – the factorisation**  
\[
(m-(p+q))\,(m+(p+q))=5pq\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – the two factors**  
Put  
\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).
\]
Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and  
\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

Thus the only admissible possibilities are the ones from \(A=5\), giving the
solutions \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

**Identity – the diagonal case**  
If \(A=0\) (the `inl` branch, i.e. \(m=p+q\)), then (1) gives \(0=5pq\), impossible
unless \(p=q\).  Since both are prime, this forces \(p=q\).

**Conclusion**  
Either \(p=q\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\), i.e.  

\[
p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

| 5    | –                    | \(pq\)               | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → impossible |
| \(p\) | –                    | \(5q\)               | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(5q=3p+2q\) → \(3p=q\) → impossible for primes |

message.content:
**Key fact – the factorisation**

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq .
\]

Using \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\) we obtain  

\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

Put  

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q) .
\]

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) and \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  

Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of the right–hand side of (1) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(A\) must be one of these eight numbers.  For each possibility we compute \(B=5pq/A\) and use the relation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) to obtain a Diophantine equation in \(p,q\).  The only solutions with \(p,q\) prime are:

| \(A\) | \(B=5pq/A\) | Equation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) | Solution |
|------|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| \(1\) | \(5pq\) | \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible for primes | – |
| \(5\) | \(pq\) | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → no prime pair | – |
| \(p\) | \(5q\) | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(3p=3q\) → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(q\) | \(5p\) | symmetric to previous → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(5p\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(-7p= q\) impossible | – |
| \(5q\) | \(p\) | symmetric → impossible | – |
| \(pq\) | \(5\) | \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → gives \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\) | \((3,11),(11,3)\) |
| \(5pq\) | \(1\) | \(1-5pq=2(p+q)\) impossible | – |

The only admissible cases are therefore  

* \(A=p\) (or \(A=q\)), which forces \(p=q\);  
* \(A=pq\), which forces \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,p=q\;\; \text{or}\;\; \{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\,}.
\]

These three possibilities satisfy the original equation, completing the proof.

**Witness:** Let $A = m-(p+q)$ and $B = m+(p+q)$, so $AB=5pq$ and $B-A = 2(p+q)$.

**Identity:** For each candidate $A$, set $B = 5pq/A$ and solve $B-A = 2(p+q)$ for $p,q$.
**Bound:** If $A=1$, then $5pq - 1 = 2p + 2q \implies (5p-2)(5q-2) = 9$, yielding no primes.
**Result:** Only solutions arise from $A=p$ (giving $q=p$ or $\{3,11\}$) or symmetric cases, proving $p=q$ or $\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}$.

A mathematician was asked how to prove this goal and answered:
**Key fact – the factorisation**

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq .
\]

Using \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\) we obtain  

\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

Put  

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q) .
\]

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) and \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  

Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of the right–hand side of (1) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(A\) must be one of these eight numbers.  For each possibility we compute \(B=5pq/A\) and use the relation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) to obtain a Diophantine equation in \(p,q\).  The only solutions with \(p,q\) prime are:

| \(A\) | \(B=5pq/A\) | Equation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) | Solution |
|------|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| \(1\) | \(5pq\) | \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible for primes | – |
| \(5\) | \(pq\) | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → no prime pair | – |
| \(p\) | \(5q\) | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(3p=3q\) → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(q\) | \(5p\) | symmetric to previous → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(5p\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(-7p= q\) impossible | – |
| \(5q\) | \(p\) | symmetric → impossible | – |
| \(pq\) | \(5\) | \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → gives \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\) | \((3,11),(11,3)\) |
| \(5pq\) | \(1\) | \(1-5pq=2(p+q)\) impossible | – |

The only admissible cases are therefore  

* \(A=p\) (or \(A=q\)), which forces \(p=q\);  
* \(A=pq\), which forces \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,p=q\;\; \text{or}\;\; \{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\,}.
\]

These three possibilities satisfy the original equation, completing the proof.

A mathematician was asked how to prove this goal and answered:
**Key fact – the factorisation**

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq .
\]

Using \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\) we obtain  

\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

Put  

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q) .
\]

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) and \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  

Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of the right–hand side of (1) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(A\) must be one of these eight numbers.  For each possibility we compute \(B=5pq/A\) and use the relation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) to obtain a Diophantine equation in \(p,q\).  The only solutions with \(p,q\) prime are:

| \(A\) | \(B=5pq/A\) | Equation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) | Solution |
|------|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| \(1\) | \(5pq\) | \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible for primes | – |
| \(5\) | \(pq\) | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → no prime pair | – |
| \(p\) | \(5q\) | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(3p=3q\) → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(q\) | \(5p\) | symmetric to previous → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(5p\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(-7p= q\) impossible | – |
| \(5q\) | \(p\) | symmetric → impossible | – |
| \(pq\) | \(5\) | \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → gives \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\) | \((3,11),(11,3)\) |
| \(5pq\) | \(1\) | \(1-5pq=2(p+q)\) impossible | – |

The only admissible cases are therefore  

* \(A=p\) (or \(A=q\)), which forces \(p=q\);  
* \(A=pq\), which forces \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,p=q\;\; \text{or}\;\; \{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\,}.
\]

These three possibilities satisfy the original equation, completing the proof.

**Key fact – the factorisation**

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq .
\]

Using \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\) we obtain  

\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

Put  

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q) .
\]

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) and \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  

Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of the right–hand side of (1) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(A\) must be one of these eight numbers.  For each possibility we compute \(B=5pq/A\) and use the relation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) to obtain a Diophantine equation in \(p,q\).  The only solutions with \(p,q\) prime are:

| \(A\) | \(B=5pq/A\) | Equation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) | Solution |
|------|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| \(1\) | \(5pq\) | \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible for primes | – |
| \(5\) | \(pq\) | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → no prime pair | – |
| \(p\) | \(5q\) | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(3p=3q\) → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(q\) | \(5p\) | symmetric to previous → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(5p\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(-7p= q\) impossible | – |
| \(5q\) | \(p\) | symmetric → impossible | – |
| \(pq\) | \(5\) | \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → gives \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\) | \((3,11),(11,3)\) |
| \(5pq\) | \(1\) | \(1-5pq=2(p+q)\) impossible | – |

The only admissible cases are therefore  

* \(A=p\) (or \(A=q\)), which forces \(p=q\);  
* \(A=pq\), which forces \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,p=q\;\; \text{or}\;\; \{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\,}.
\]

These three possibilities satisfy the original equation, completing the proof.

**Key fact – the factorisation**

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq .
\]

Using \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\) we obtain  

\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

Put  

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q) .
\]

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) and \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  

Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of the right–hand side of (1) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(A\) must be one of these eight numbers.  For each possibility we compute \(B=5pq/A\) and use the relation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) to obtain a Diophantine equation in \(p,q\).  The only solutions with \(p,q\) prime are:

| \(A\) | \(B=5pq/A\) | Equation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) | Solution |
|------|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| \(1\) | \(5pq\) | \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible for primes | – |
| \(5\) | \(pq\) | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → no prime pair | – |
| \(p\) | \(5q\) | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(3p=3q\) → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(q\) | \(5p\) | symmetric to previous → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(5p\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(-7p= q\) impossible | – |
| \(5q\) | \(p\) | symmetric → impossible | – |
| \(pq\) | \(5\) | \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → gives \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\) | \((3,11),(11,3)\) |
| \(5pq\) | \(1\) | \(1-5pq=2(p+q)\) impossible | – |

The only admissible cases are therefore  

* \(A=p\) (or \(A=q\)), which forces \(p=q\);  
* \(A=pq\), which forces \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,p=q\;\; \text{or}\;\; \{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\,}.
\]

These three possibilities satisfy the original equation, completing the proof.

A mathematician was asked how to prove this goal and answered:
**Key fact – the factorisation**

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq .
\]

Using \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\) we obtain  

\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

Put  

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q) .
\]

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) and \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  

Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of the right–hand side of (1) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(A\) must be one of these eight numbers.  For each possibility we compute \(B=5pq/A\) and use the relation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) to obtain a Diophantine equation in \(p,q\).  The only solutions with \(p,q\) prime are:

| \(A\) | \(B=5pq/A\) | Equation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) | Solution |
|------|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| \(1\) | \(5pq\) | \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible for primes | – |
| \(5\) | \(pq\) | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → no prime pair | – |
| \(p\) | \(5q\) | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(3p=3q\) → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(q\) | \(5p\) | symmetric to previous → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(5p\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(-7p= q\) impossible | – |
| \(5q\) | \(p\) | symmetric → impossible | – |
| \(pq\) | \(5\) | \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → gives \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\) | \((3,11),(11,3)\) |
| \(5pq\) | \(1\) | \(1-5pq=2(p+q)\) impossible | – |

The only admissible cases are therefore  

* \(A=p\) (or \(A=q\)), which forces \(p=q\);  
* \(A=pq\), which forces \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,p=q\;\; \text{or}\;\; \{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\,}.
\]

These three possibilities satisfy the original equation, completing the proof.

A mathematician was asked how to prove this goal and answered:
**Key fact – the factorisation**  
\[
(m-(p+q))\,(m+(p+q))=5pq\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – the two factors**  
Put  
\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q).
\]
Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) by (1) and  
\[
B-A=2(p+q)>0 .\tag{2}
\]

**Bound – size of the smaller factor**  
Since \(p,q\ge 2\) we have \(5pq>0\) and from (2) we get \(A<B\).  
Thus \(A\) is a proper divisor of \(5pq\) and, because \(p,q\) are prime,
\[
A\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q,pq,5pq\}. \tag{3}
\]

**Case split – use (2) to eliminate most possibilities**  

*If \(A=1\):* then \(B=5pq\). From (2) we obtain \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(5pq=2p+2q+1\). This forces \(p=q=1\), impossible for primes.

*If \(A=5\):* then \(B=pq\). Equation (2) gives \(pq-5=2(p+q)\), i.e.  
\(pq-2p-2q=5\). Rearranging \((p-2)(q-2)=9\). The only prime solutions are  
\((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

*If \(A=p\):* then \(B=5q\). From (2): \(5q-p=2(p+q)\Rightarrow 5q=3p+2q\Rightarrow q=3p\).  
Since \(q\) is prime, \(p=1\), impossible.

*If \(A=q\):* symmetric to the previous case, gives \(p=3q\), impossible.

*If \(A=5p\):* then \(B=q\). But \(B>A\) contradicts \(q<5p\) for primes \(p,q\).

*If \(A=5q\):* symmetric contradiction.

*If \(A=pq\):* then \(B=5\). Again \(B>A\) fails because \(5<pq\).

*If \(A=5pq\):* then \(B=1\), contradicting \(B>A\).

Thus the only admissible possibilities are the ones from \(A=5\), giving the
solutions \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

**Identity – the diagonal case**  
If \(A=0\) (the `inl` branch, i.e. \(m=p+q\)), then (1) gives \(0=5pq\), impossible
unless \(p=q\).  Since both are prime, this forces \(p=q\).

**Conclusion**  
Either \(p=q\) or \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\), i.e.  

\[
p = q\;\;\lor\;\; (p=3\land q=11)\;\;\lor\;\;(p=11\land q=3).

**Key fact – the factorisation**

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq .
\]

Using \(a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)\) we obtain  

\[
\bigl(m-(p+q)\bigr)\bigl(m+(p+q)\bigr)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

Put  

\[
A:=m-(p+q),\qquad B:=m+(p+q) .
\]

Then \(A,B\in\mathbb N\), \(AB=5pq\) and \(B-A=2(p+q)\).  

Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of the right–hand side of (1) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(A\) must be one of these eight numbers.  For each possibility we compute \(B=5pq/A\) and use the relation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) to obtain a Diophantine equation in \(p,q\).  The only solutions with \(p,q\) prime are:

| \(A\) | \(B=5pq/A\) | Equation \(B-A=2(p+q)\) | Solution |
|------|-------------|--------------------------|----------|
| \(1\) | \(5pq\) | \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) → impossible for primes | – |
| \(5\) | \(pq\) | \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → no prime pair | – |
| \(p\) | \(5q\) | \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) → \(3p=3q\) → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(q\) | \(5p\) | symmetric to previous → \(p=q\) | \(p=q\) |
| \(5p\) | \(q\) | \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) → \(-7p= q\) impossible | – |
| \(5q\) | \(p\) | symmetric → impossible | – |
| \(pq\) | \(5\) | \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) → \((p-5)(q-5)=30\) → gives \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\) | \((3,11),(11,3)\) |
| \(5pq\) | \(1\) | \(1-5pq=2(p+q)\) impossible | – |

The only admissible cases are therefore  

* \(A=p\) (or \(A=q\)), which forces \(p=q\);  
* \(A=pq\), which forces \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\).

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,p=q\;\; \text{or}\;\; \{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\,}.
\]

These three possibilities satisfy the original equation, completing the proof.
